Rollback expectations: time-to-rollback, blast radius, safe defaults

Change approvals: RBAC, justification, ticket linking, separation of duties
Progressive delivery: canary apply and metric gates
Comms and runbooks: who gets paged and what links are included

Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: HelixBank x Redwood — post-incident review (Optimize config rollback expectations)
Recorded: 2024-11-12 18:00:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees:
- Elliot Price (Redwood Inference)
- Rafael Mendes (Redwood Inference)
- Allison Grant (Redwood Inference)
- Fiona McCarthy (Redwood Inference)
- Anika Sharma (HelixBank)
- David Kim (HelixBank)
- Laura Chen (HelixBank)
- Miguel Torres (HelixBank)

Auto-summary (generated)
- HelixBank recapped an incident where an optimization configuration change (batching/quantization-related) correlated with a p95 latency spike and elevated 5xx errors.
- HelixBank expects rollback to be executable by on-call within minutes, with clear blast radius, progress/status, and a way to prove what changed (diff + version history).
- HelixBank requires strong RBAC, immutable audit logs, ticket linkage, and export to SIEM; they prefer rollback to remain available during incident response without extra approval bottlenecks.
- Redwood previewed the upcoming “safe apply + rollback” workflow: preflight validation, diff/preview, canary + metric gates, and one-click rollback to a known-good version.

Action items (generated)
- Redwood to send draft runbook + screenshots of console flow.
- Redwood to share audit event schema sample payloads and retention options.
- HelixBank to provide CAB/change-management fields and confirm rollback RTO + authorized roles.

Transcript

[00:00] Elliot Price: Hey everyone. Thanks for making time. This is Elliot from Redwood, customer success on our side. I’ve got Rafael from on-call/SRE, Allison from observability, and Fiona from security ops. The goal today is to do a quick post-incident review, but mostly to capture your expectations for rollback: time, visibility, approvals, audit, all that.

[00:24] Anika Sharma: Yep. Appreciate it. We’re not here to point fingers, but we do want to make sure we never do this again, or at least we can undo it quickly.

[00:34] Miguel Torres: Yeah. The practical thing is: we lost like— what was it— 20 to 25 minutes of degraded service while we were figuring out what knob got changed.

[00:43] Rafael Mendes: Totally. I pulled the internal timeline. We can share a redacted version. The key point is the config change and the latency spike line up basically within minutes.

[00:53] David Kim: To be specific, it was after we applied the Optimize recommendation, right? The “cost saver” thing.

[01:00] Elliot Price: Yeah, that’s my understanding. It was an Optimize config change applied to your Dedicated deployment, your prod route group.

[01:07] Anika Sharma: In our notes, we see it as a batching change plus a quant profile flip. And then p95 just went vertical.

[01:15] Allison Grant: We saw that too on the Redwood side. The p95 panel jumped and the error rate climbed. The tricky bit was correlating it quickly to “this exact config version changed.” That’s like… exactly why we’re building the history + rollback.

[01:30] Laura Chen: Before we get into tooling— our main gap was governance. Who can apply those changes, and how do we capture approvals.

[01:38] Elliot Price: Yep. Let’s do it in two parts: (1) your operational expectations during an incident, and (2) your compliance/change mgmt expectations in steady state.

[01:49] Elliot Price: Anika, from SRE perspective— what’s the rollback target? Like if you see the regression, how fast do you want to be back to known-good?

[01:59] Anika Sharma: If you’re asking “RTO for rollback,” we want <5 minutes from decision to back to stable. Realistically: detect within 2–3 minutes, rollback within another 2–3.

[02:11] Rafael Mendes: That’s aligned with what we’re targeting internally: rollback should be a one-click operation for authorized on-call and complete in minutes, not tens of minutes.

[02:20] David Kim: But it can’t be one click into the void. We need to see blast radius and progress. Like is it applied to all clusters? Did one shard get stuck?

[02:30] Allison Grant: +1. We’re adding propagation status reporting. The idea is you see “in progress / completed / failed” per region/cluster.

[02:39] Miguel Torres: And if it fails halfway through, we cannot end up with two configs live. Split brain is worse.

[02:46] Rafael Mendes: 100%. That’s a core requirement. Atomic semantics per scope. If it can’t complete, it should fail safe, and you should be able to retry idempotently.

[02:56] David Kim: Idempotent meaning if I click rollback twice it doesn’t do something new.

[02:59] Rafael Mendes: Exactly. Same request id, same outcome.

[03:04] Elliot Price: Ok. Let’s talk “what you need on screen” when you’re doing it. During the incident, what did you not have that you wish you had?

[03:13] Anika Sharma: Honestly, a timeline. “At 10:42 this config changed, by this person, from X to Y.” Not a Slack archaeology situation.

[03:23] David Kim: Diff would have helped. We had to compare JSON blobs manually. And there are nested fields; you don’t know which one matters.

[03:33] Miguel Torres: Also context: which route and which model. Because we have multiple models behind the same product endpoint.

[03:40] Elliot Price: So version history at the scope level: route/model/customer deployment. With metadata.

[03:45] Laura Chen: And it needs to be immutable. No editing past versions.

[03:48] Fiona McCarthy: Yep. We’re designing it as an append-only history with immutable version records. You can add a new version, but you can’t rewrite old ones.

[03:58] Laura Chen: Good.

[04:00] Elliot Price: What about rollback permissions? Who should be allowed to rollback?

[04:05] Anika Sharma: On-call SREs need the ability. Not everyone in app engineering. But during an incident we can’t wait for a product admin to wake up.

[04:14] Laura Chen: This is important: we typically require “two-person rule” for changes, but rollback is different. Rollback is remediation. We allow break-glass under incident declaration, with audit.

[04:26] Fiona McCarthy: That’s consistent with what we see in other regulated customers. Break-glass roles with heavy logging.

[04:33] David Kim: But still, we want the system to prompt for a reason. Like “INC-1234” ticket number. Otherwise we lose traceability.

[04:42] Elliot Price: Got it. So: require justification string + ticket link on apply and rollback. And store it with the version event.

[04:49] Miguel Torres: Yes.

[04:51] Allison Grant: We can include that in audit events too. The audit record includes actor, time, scope, old_version, new_version, reason, and a correlation id.

[05:02] David Kim: Correlation id is key because we want to tie this back to our metrics and logs.

[05:07] Allison Grant: Exactly. We’ll also emit metrics like config_apply_success and config_apply_latency with that id.

[05:16] Anika Sharma: During the incident, we had a hard time proving “rollback fixed it.” We rolled back two knobs and it got better, but we couldn’t quickly show it.

[05:26] Rafael Mendes: What would “proof” look like for you? A checklist? A dashboard view?

[05:31] Anika Sharma: Dashboard that overlays config change events on latency/error graphs. And a runbook: after rollback, check p95, check error rate, check saturation.

[05:43] Allison Grant: That’s literally what we’re building in the dashboard pack: event overlays and a “change health” panel.

[05:50] Miguel Torres: We also care about output quality. Like quant changes can degrade responses. Not always immediate. Do you have gates for that?

[06:00] Elliot Price: In the first release, we’re focusing on metric gates for latency and error. Quality gating is possible, but it’s not fully automated yet. We can integrate eval signals where you have them.

[06:12] David Kim: So no auto-rollback based on quality drop.

[06:15] Elliot Price: Not in initial GA. But safe-apply can surface warnings, and you can do canary with gates. Quality signals can be part of those gates if you have a measurable proxy.

[06:26] Miguel Torres: Ok.

[06:28] Elliot Price: Can we go back to what exactly happened? Just to ensure we capture the “why rollback needed.”

[06:34] David Kim: Sure. We applied an Optimize recommendation Friday. It increased batch size max and turned on… I think prefix cache? Or it changed cache TTL. The transcript might be wrong but it was cache-related.

[06:49] Rafael Mendes: I see in our notes it bumped the continuous batching window and changed a quantization profile from fp16 to something like int8. I might be mixing it up.

[07:00] David Kim: Yeah, it was int8. And then we saw a bunch of timeouts.

[07:04] Anika Sharma: Timeouts plus 502s from our gateway.

[07:08] Allison Grant: We saw the engine reporting queue depth spikes. That’s consistent with too aggressive batching / scheduler.

[07:17] Miguel Torres: Right. So our expectation: If you push that kind of change, the platform should stop you, or at least warn you. Not “apply and pray.”

[07:27] Elliot Price: Understood. That’s where preflight validation comes in.

[07:32] Laura Chen: Validation should also enforce policy. Like “in prod, you can’t change quant profile without a canary” or “requires approval.”

[07:41] Fiona McCarthy: We can support policy guardrails: require canary for certain fields; require specific permission; require justification; block if outside bounds.

[07:52] David Kim: Can we define the bounds? Because for our traffic pattern, batch size above a certain number is just dangerous.

[07:59] Rafael Mendes: We can provide safe defaults and allow per-tenant overrides, within reason. The validator can flag “high risk” changes.

[08:09] Anika Sharma: But I also want a fast path: if I’m in incident response, I should not need to pass ten checks. Rollback should be easy.

[08:18] Elliot Price: That makes sense. We treat rollback as reverting to a known-good version; preflight can be lighter, but we’ll still do schema validation and compatibility checks.

[08:29] David Kim: And rollback should invalidate caches if needed. We saw weird behavior where even after changing config, it took time to settle.

[08:39] Rafael Mendes: Yup. There are runtime edge cases. Cache invalidation and warmup behavior matter. We’re adding explicit steps so rollback doesn’t leave stale KV cache behavior.

[08:50] Miguel Torres: We’d like that documented. Like “rollback resets X, Y, but Z may take 2 minutes to normalize.”

[08:57] Elliot Price: We can include that in the runbook and known-issues section.

[09:02] Laura Chen: On audit: we need export to Splunk. And retention at least 1 year, maybe 7 years for some events. We can discuss.

[09:14] Fiona McCarthy: We can support long retention for audit logs on enterprise tiers and export via webhook/SIEM integration. We’ll also discuss redaction rules— for example, we won’t log prompt content, but we will log config fields changed.

[09:28] Laura Chen: Ok. We don’t want any customer data in audit logs, but config metadata is fine.

[09:34] Allison Grant: And audit logs will include “where applied” like region/cluster IDs, but not payload data.

[09:43] David Kim: Another expectation: change approvals. We use ServiceNow for CAB. We want the UI to force a ticket number, and ideally API should enforce it too.

[09:55] Elliot Price: Understood. For the API endpoints, we can require a “reason” and “ticket_url” field. And RBAC ensures only certain roles can apply.

[10:06] Anika Sharma: Also separation of duties. The person who creates a new version shouldn’t necessarily be able to apply it to prod.

[10:14] Fiona McCarthy: That’s doable with separate permissions: create vs apply vs rollback.

[10:19] David Kim: Great.

[10:21] Elliot Price: Let’s talk canary apply. Do you want every config change canaried first?

[10:27] Anika Sharma: For prod: yes. At least for the high-risk knobs.

[10:32] Miguel Torres: For a new quant profile, definitely yes. For like a cache TTL maybe canary but it depends.

[10:40] Allison Grant: We’re building canary as an option, and policy can require it for specific field changes.

[10:48] David Kim: What metrics do you gate on?

[10:51] Allison Grant: Default is p95 latency, error rate, and sometimes saturation. We can align to your SLOs.

[10:59] Anika Sharma: We’d want p95 latency +20% max for canary, and error rate not above baseline + maybe 0.2%. Something like that.

[11:09] Rafael Mendes: That’s in line with what we’ve heard. We’ll confirm exact numbers and per-tier differences.

[11:17] Miguel Torres: And time window. It has to bake long enough to catch issues.

[11:22] Allison Grant: Typically 10–15 minutes for canary, or N requests, whichever first. We can tune.

[11:32] David Kim: Ok.

[11:34] Elliot Price: Switching to comms: during the incident, who did you want notified and how?

[11:41] Anika Sharma: Our #prod-llm-oncall Slack channel. We also need an email to the incident ticket sometimes.

[11:47] David Kim: And we want the message to include a rollback deep link. Like literally “click here to rollback to v12.”

[11:55] Rafael Mendes: That’s planned. The incident bot will post config change events with rollback link and correlation id.

[12:03] Miguel Torres: Nice.

[12:05] Laura Chen: For compliance: we also need an audit trail for attempted changes, not just successful ones.

[12:12] Fiona McCarthy: Yes. We log attempted/apply, applied, failed; same for rollback. Including failure reasons.

[12:20] Laura Chen: Great.

[12:22] Elliot Price: I want to sanity check: whole-config rollback is what we’re initially shipping. Is that acceptable?

[12:29] David Kim: Meaning we revert the entire optimize config blob back to a previous version.

[12:34] Elliot Price: Right.

[12:35] David Kim: That’s fine as long as we can see the diff. Partial rollback could be nice but we can live without it initially.

[12:42] Anika Sharma: Agree. In an incident, you want “known good.” Not surgery.

[12:48] Miguel Torres: Yeah, but we need to know what “known good” means. Like how do you mark versions as good?

[12:54] Rafael Mendes: Great question. We can tag versions as “active” and optionally “pinned.” Known-good is basically last active stable version; we can also allow marking a version as “approved.”

[13:07] Laura Chen: “Approved” flag would be great for audits.

[13:10] Fiona McCarthy: We can include an approval workflow later; for now, we can capture ticket linkage and role-based permissions.

[13:19] David Kim: Another question: Can we do rollback via API? Not only via console.

[13:24] Elliot Price: Yes. There will be an endpoint to rollback to a specific version. And list versions. Console uses the same.

[13:33] David Kim: Perfect. We have automation on our side.

[13:36] Anika Sharma: But you should still limit it. API tokens need to be scoped, maybe per environment.

[13:43] Fiona McCarthy: Yes. RBAC and token scoping applies; and we recommend short-lived credentials via SSO where possible.

[13:51] Laura Chen: We use SAML for SSO. Just confirming that will work.

[13:54] Fiona McCarthy: Yes, for Console access. For API, we’ll align with your preferred auth model; we can discuss.

[14:01] Elliot Price: Ok. Let’s capture the “definition of done” from your perspective.

[14:06] Anika Sharma: For me:
1) Version history with who/what/when.
2) One-click rollback with progress and blast radius.
3) Rollback in under 5 minutes.
4) Audit logs exported.
5) Canary + gates for risky changes.

[14:24] David Kim: Add: diff preview. And correlation ID that shows up in dashboards.

[14:30] Laura Chen: Add: enforce ticket/justification and separation of duties.

[14:36] Miguel Torres: Add: documentation for runtime behavior, cache invalidation, warmup times. So we can explain it internally.

[14:46] Elliot Price: Great. On the “blast radius” display— what do you want that to look like?

[14:52] David Kim: Something like: “This will apply to: HelixBank prod, us-east, cluster A/B/C, routes /chat and /summary, models Llama-3.1-70B and embeddings.” You know what I mean.

[15:07] Rafael Mendes: Yep, a scope summary.

[15:09] Anika Sharma: And confirm there isn’t any other tenant impacted. We’re Dedicated but we still want assurance.

[15:16] Elliot Price: Understood.

[15:19] Allison Grant: During incident response, would you want the rollback UI to show “expected recovery” or recommended checks?

[15:26] Anika Sharma: Yes. Like a checklist with links. Otherwise people forget.

[15:31] Rafael Mendes: We can include that in the post-rollback view.

[15:35] David Kim: One more thing: we had to involve Redwood to understand which knobs changed. We want to self-serve.

[15:43] Elliot Price: That’s the goal.

[15:46] Laura Chen: And access logs. We need to know which Redwood internal users accessed our config.

[15:52] Fiona McCarthy: We can include admin access events in audit logs as well (support access). There are policies around that.

[16:00] Laura Chen: Great.

[16:02] Elliot Price: Ok, I think we have the core requirements. Before we close, anything else that would have made Friday smoother?

[16:10] Anika Sharma: Better alerting. Like config apply failures or stuck rollout should page us.

[16:16] Allison Grant: We’re adding alerts for elevated failure rate and stuck applies.

[16:21] Miguel Torres: And maybe guardrails so Optimize doesn’t recommend a config that violates our SLO.

[16:28] Elliot Price: That’s in the roadmap too— safer recommendations and preflight checks.

[16:33] David Kim: Ok.

[16:34] Elliot Price: Last thing: timeline. We’re aiming to have version history + rollback in beta soon, then safe-apply with preflight and canary gates next. I’ll follow up with dates, but it’s weeks, not quarters.

[16:47] Anika Sharma: Good. We’ll hold you to the <5 minute rollback.

[16:51] Rafael Mendes: Please do.

[16:53] Elliot Price: Cool. Recap: We’ll send runbook drafts and UI notes, and we’ll set up a security follow-up for audit event schema + SIEM export. Thanks everyone.

[17:05] Laura Chen: Thanks.

[17:06] David Kim: Thanks.

[17:07] Anika Sharma: Thanks.

[17:08] Miguel Torres: Thanks.

[17:10] (Meeting ends)

Note: Some speaker attribution may be inaccurate due to transcription.
